metadata.title: Algebraic Identities and Decimal Shortcuts
metadata.description: Use algebraic identities and factorization to simplify decimal expressions efficiently.
metadata.teachingApproach: Teach through short, connected phone-sized screens: a concrete idea, worked steps on separate lines, a reason and check, then fresh practice. Wrong answers receive a worked correction and a parallel retry that must be answered correctly before the lesson advances.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 3 Decimal Fractions: the identities listed in Important Facts and Formulae on printed page 70 and solved examples 20-25 on printed pages 73-74, with later objective patterns that apply those same identities. No identities beyond the approved list are introduced.

content.text:
Let's spot shortcuts hidden inside long decimal expressions.

For example, 12.4² − 7.6² looks like two large squares. The numbers also make an easy sum and difference. An identity lets us use those easier parts.

A difference of two complete squares can be factored:

a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b).

Why? Multiply the brackets: a² − ab + ab − b². The middle terms cancel.

Try 12.4² − 7.6².

Sum: 12.4 + 7.6 = 20
Difference: 12.4 − 7.6 = 4.8
Product: 20 × 4.8 = 96.

Check size: 12² − 8² = 80, so 96 is reasonable. Do not replace a² − b² with (a − b)²; that is a different expression.
Evaluate 78.95² − 43.35² using an identity.

Check for two squared terms separated by subtraction. Apply (a+b)(a−b); do not square the difference itself.

(78.95 + 43.35)(78.95 − 43.35) = 122.30 × 35.60 = 4,353.88.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
Evaluate 36.54² − 3.46².

Let’s check this one.

Factor as (36.54 + 3.46)(36.54 − 3.46).

40 × 33.08 = 1,323.2.

Try the same question again and check the result.

When two quantities are added before squaring, both cross-products appear:

(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b².

The middle term is twice a times b.

For 2.01², write 2.01 = 2 + 0.01:

2² + 2(2)(0.01) + 0.01²
= 4 + 0.04 + 0.0001
= 4.0401.

Check: a number just over 2 has a square just over 4. Omitting 2ab would give too little.
Evaluate (3.02)² using an identity.

hints: Use (a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; include the middle term.

content.text:
A squared sum includes the middle term 2ab.

(3 + 0.02)² = 3² + 2(3)(0.02) + 0.02² = 9.1204. Check that the result is a little over 9, then use the same pattern with new values.
Evaluate (2.03)².

Let’s check this one.

Write 2.03 as 2 + 0.03.

4 + 0.12 + 0.0009 = 4.1209.

Try the same question again and check the result.

When we subtract before squaring, the middle term is negative:

(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².

The last square remains positive.

For 0.97², use 0.97 = 1 − 0.03:

1 − 2(1)(0.03) + 0.03²
= 1 − 0.06 + 0.0009
= 0.9409.

Check: a number below 1 has a square below 1. Use the sign of the middle term carefully.
Evaluate (0.98)².

For (a−b)², the middle term is −2ab. Substitute 1 and 0.02 carefully: 1 − 0.04 + 0.0004.

(1 − 0.02)² = 1 − 0.04 + 0.0004 = 0.9604.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
Evaluate (0.99)² using an identity.

inlineData.explanation: (1 − 0.01)² = 1 − 0.02 + 0.0001 = 0.9801. Check: a number below 1 has a square below 1.

content.text:
For a squared difference, subtract the cross-term but add the small final square.

(1 − 0.01)² = 1 − 0.02 + 0.0001 = 0.9801. Try the question again.

Three terms make three squares and three pairs of cross-products:

(a+b+c)² = a²+b²+c²+2ab+2bc+2ca.

Each pair appears twice when the brackets are multiplied.

Let a=0.2, b=0.3, c=0.4. Their sum is 0.9, so the square is 0.81.

Expanded check:
0.04+0.09+0.16+0.12+0.24+0.16 = 0.81.

Spot all three cross-pairs before choosing this identity. Adding only the squares would give 0.29, far too small.

hints: Match the six terms to a²+b²+c²+2ab+2bc+2ca.

content.text:
Match all six terms to a²+b²+c²+2ab+2bc+2ca. Here that is (0.6+0.4+0.3)² = 1.3² = 1.69.

The complete three-term-square identity gives (1.3)² = 1.69.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.

hints: Group each square and each doubled pairwise product.
inlineData.explanation: The expression is the full square (1.5)² = 2.25.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

Group each square and each doubled pairwise product.

The expression is the full square (1.5)² = 2.25.

Try the same question again and check the result.

Two cubes added have a useful factor:

a³+b³ = (a+b)(a²−ab+b²).

The middle sign in the second bracket is minus.

If an expression is

(0.02³+0.03³)/(0.02²−0.02×0.03+0.03²),

the denominator is the matching second factor. Cancel that whole nonzero factor. The value is 0.02+0.03 = 0.05. Check the signs and the full factor before cancelling.

hints: Recognize a³ + b³ in the numerator.
The denominator is its matching factor; add a+b.

content.text:
Match numerator and denominator to the sum-of-cubes identity. The common factor a² − ab + b² cancels, leaving a+b, when it is nonzero.

By a³+b³=(a+b)(a²−ab+b²), the quotient is 0.051 + 0.041 = 0.092.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.

hints: The common quadratic factor cancels; add 0.013 and 0.007.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

Use the sum-of-cubes factorization.

The quotient equals 0.013 + 0.007 = 0.020.

Try the same question again and check the result.

For cubes subtracted, the signs change:

a³−b³ = (a−b)(a²+ab+b²).

The second bracket uses plus signs.

If the denominator is exactly a²+ab+b², the quotient of the cube difference by that denominator is a−b.

With a=4.2 and b=1.8, the result is 2.4. Check: 4.2−1.8=2.4. We cancel a common factor, never separate terms inside a sum.

inlineData.explanation: The matching quadratic factor cancels, leaving 5.71 − 2.79 = 2.92.

content.text:
For a³ − b³, use (a−b)(a²+ab+b²). The denominator is the matching second factor, so the quotient is a−b.

The matching quadratic factor cancels, leaving 5.71 − 2.79 = 2.92.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.

Let’s check this one.

Use the difference-of-cubes factorization.

The quotient is 2.3 − 0.3 = 2.

Try the same question again and check the result.

For three values, the book's identity is:

a³+b³+c³−3abc
= (a+b+c)(a²+b²+c²−ab−bc−ca).

The special case a+b+c=0 makes the right side zero.

Then a³+b³+c³ = 3abc.

Take a=0.1, b=0.2, c=−0.3. Their sum is zero. So the cube sum is 3(0.1)(0.2)(−0.3) = −0.018.

Check directly: 0.001+0.008−0.027 = −0.018. Test the zero-sum condition first.
If a=0.2, b=0.3, and c=−0.5, find a³+b³+c³.

inlineData.prompt: If a=0.2, b=0.3, and c=−0.5, find a³+b³+c³.
inlineData.explanation: The sum is zero, so a³+b³+c³=3abc=3(0.2)(0.3)(−0.5)=−0.09.

content.text:
First verify a+b+c=0. Only then use a³+b³+c³=3abc. Here 0.2 + 0.3 − 0.5 = 0.

The sum is zero, so a³+b³+c³=3abc=3(0.2)(0.3)(−0.5)=−0.09.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
If x=0.4, y=0.1, and z=−0.5, find x³+y³+z³.

inlineData.prompt: If x=0.4, y=0.1, and z=−0.5, find x³+y³+z³.
inlineData.explanation: Since x+y+z=0, the sum of cubes is 3xyz = 3(0.4)(0.1)(−0.5) = −0.06.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

Their sum is 0.4 + 0.1 − 0.5 = 0.

Since x+y+z=0, the sum of cubes is 3xyz = 3(0.4)(0.1)(−0.5) = −0.06.

Try the same question again and check the result.

When a quotient contains a cube difference and its matching quadratic factor, focus on the pattern before the decimal arithmetic.

Let a=3.6 and b=2.4. The quotient (a³−b³)/(a²+ab+b²) has that exact pattern.

Factor the numerator:

(a−b)(a²+ab+b²).

Cancel the common nonzero factor. The result is a−b = 3.6−2.4 = 1.2.

These values are easy to subtract. The identity saves the cube calculations, but only when every sign and term matches.

hints: This is a quotient from the difference-of-cubes identity.

content.text:
Match the cube difference and its denominator to the identity. The result is 2.75 − 2.25 = 0.5.

The quotient simplifies to 2.75 − 2.25 = 0.5.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.

Let’s check this one.

Recognize the sum-of-cubes pattern.

The quotient is 0.943 + 0.057 = 1.

Try the same question again and check the result.

Cancellation works on factors joined by multiplication, not on individual terms joined by plus or minus.

For (a²−b²)/(a−b), first factor the numerator.

a²−b² = (a−b)(a+b).

If a−b is not zero, cancel that whole factor. The quotient is a+b.

With a=1.5 and b=0.5, the original is (2.25−0.25)/1 = 2, matching 1.5+0.5. If a=b, the original denominator is zero and cancellation is not allowed.
For a ≠ b, simplify (a² − b²)/(a − b).

inlineData.prompt: For a ≠ b, simplify (a² − b²)/(a − b).
hints: Cancel the common factor a−b, which is nonzero here.

content.text:
Factor the whole numerator first. Cancel only an identical nonzero factor appearing multiplicatively in numerator and denominator.

(a²−b²)/(a−b) = (a−b)(a+b)/(a−b) = a+b, provided a≠b.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
Which operation is valid when simplifying (x² + 3x)/x, for x ≠ 0?

options.label: Cancel x from x² + 3x without factoring

inlineData.prompt: Which operation is valid when simplifying (x² + 3x)/x, for x ≠ 0?

options.label: Cancel x from x² + 3x without factoring

hints: Factor the numerator as a product.
Then cancel the common nonzero factor x.
inlineData.explanation: x²+3x = x(x+3), so division by x gives x+3 when x is nonzero.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

Factor the numerator as a product.

x²+3x = x(x+3), so division by x gives x+3 when x is nonzero.

Try the same question again and check the result.

The middle term can reveal a perfect square. Look for two square terms and exactly twice their product between them:

a²+2ab+b² = (a+b)².

For 3.25² + 2(3.25)(0.75) + 0.75², the two values add to 4.

So the expression is 4² = 16. Check that the middle term really is 2 × 3.25 × 0.75. A similar-looking expression with a different coefficient needs a different calculation.

hints: Match the terms to a² + 2ab + b².

content.text:
Compare the middle term with 2ab. Here the expression is a²+2ab+b², so it equals (a+b)².

The expression is (7.5 + 2.5)² = 10² = 100.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.

Let’s check this one.

This matches a² − 2ab + b².

(3.6 − 0.4)² = 3.2² = 10.24.

Try the same question again and check the result.

Before using a shortcut, name the shape you see.

Two squares subtracted? Use a²−b².
A squared sum or difference? Check its middle term.
Two cubes? Check the signs in the quadratic factor.

For a³−b³, the matching factorization is (a−b)(a²+ab+b²).

For a³+b³, it is (a+b)(a²−ab+b²). The signs are easy to swap by mistake. Test a simple value such as a=2, b=1 if you are unsure which identity matches.
Which identity directly factors a³ − b³?

inlineData.prompt: Which identity directly factors a³ − b³?
hints: A difference of cubes has a difference as the first factor.
The quadratic factor has all positive signs.

content.text:
Name the identity, verify its conditions, substitute the values, then check sign and scale. Do not choose a formula from a visual resemblance alone.

a³−b³=(a−b)(a²+ab+b²).

Use the same idea with a new set of values.
When may a³+b³+c³ be replaced by 3abc?

inlineData.prompt: When may a³+b³+c³ be replaced by 3abc?
hints: Check the condition on the sum of the three values.
inlineData.explanation: The identity gives a³+b³+c³=3abc only when a+b+c=0.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

Use the special three-variable identity.

The identity gives a³+b³+c³=3abc only when a+b+c=0.

Try the same question again and check the result.

You can recognize square and cube identities, use the zero-sum condition, and cancel only complete nonzero factors.

Before calculating, match every term and sign. After simplifying, check the value's size with an easy estimate or substitution.

A long fraction may contain the same factor at different decimal scales. Look for a sum or difference repeated above and below.

For [(12.5−7.5)(1.25+0.75)]/[(12.5+7.5)(12.5−7.5)], the factor 12.5−7.5 appears in both places.

It is 5, so it is safe to cancel. The remaining fraction is:

(1.25+0.75)/(12.5+7.5)
= 2/20 = 0.1.

Check the denominator was not zero. Do not cancel a single 12.5 from inside a sum; only complete common factors cancel.

hints: Compute the four sums and differences in pairs.
The denominator factors are ten times the matching numerator factors.
inlineData.explanation: The paired factors are 6.91/69.1 = 1/10 and 18.617/186.17 = 1/10. Their product is 1/100.

content.text:
Pair the corresponding factors: 6.91 is one tenth of 69.1, and 18.617 is one tenth of 186.17. Multiplying those two ratios gives 1/100.

The paired factors are 6.91/69.1 = 1/10 and 18.617/186.17 = 1/10. Their product is 1/100.

Use the same idea with a new set of values.

hints: Each numerator factor is one tenth of its matching denominator factor.

content.text:
Let’s check this one.

Compare 1.2 with 12, and 1.6 with 16.

(1.2/12)(1.6/16) = (1/10)(1/10) = 1/100.

Try the same question again and check the result.
